chapter: Looking back and the New York years
title: Who counts as an artist: quiet arrangers and tenors
summary: Smith names Parker, Lester, Durham, Barefield, Webster and Evans as artists and says the best are quiet.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Do you think Charlie Parker was an artist?
See, I think you're an artist.

Eddie Durham, Eddie Barefield, Ben Webster. All of them cats. Hershel Evans. All them tenor saxes. All of them artists. And mostly every guy that can play a lot of music, you just watch... I don't care what kind of an instrument he played. He's always quiet. He's not rowdy.

Yeah. Quiet. Yes, I've seen them come around and sit around... And great arrangers(?). He comes to the dance hall. Or you don't have to go the dance hall, but he'll go anywhere where there's some guy playing going on, he'll go down and sit way over in the corner. And most of the time he ain't go no horn with him. He don't have to be bothered. When he comes down, he's quiet, like ain't nothin' to it. Like what's that boy's name who play all that trumpet? He's a great arranger now. Thad.

Thad Jones. He used to be around here. He came here with a band that broke up here, maybe the Cotton Pickers... But all them guys. Ben Smith, Eddie Durham, and Henry...what's that boy's name?...Henry... All them were quiet. Jesse Stone.
Would you describe Charlie Parker as quiet?
Yeah, he's quiet to a certain extent. Yeah.
Later on he wasn't so quiet.
Well, he might have changed a little after he got to New York; after he got up there and stayed up there. Yeah, he probably changed. But he was quiet around Kansas City. He wasn't rowdy at all.
